Twenty Third Indian Antarctic Expedition
Ministry of Earth Sciences, Technical Publication No. 21, pp 71-82
Diurnal and Seasonal Variability in Carbon Monoxide 
at Maitri, Antarctica
Pavan S. Kulkarni*n, S.L. Jain1 , B.C. Aryaf, Sachin D Ghude+ , Ashok Kumar1
and Shahnawaz*
tRadio and Atmospheric Sciences Division, National Physical Laboratory,
New Delhi -  110012
^Dept. of Physics and Astrophysics, University of Delhi,
Delhi - 110007
*Email: pavannpl@yahoo.co.in
ABSTRACT
Measurement of carbon monoxide (CO) has been carried out from a pristine 
site, Maitri, (70.77° S, 11.43° E) Antarctica. The obtained time series data for one 
year period (January- December 2004) clearly indicates the occurrence of definite 
diurnal and seasonal variation of CO concentration in ambient air at Antarctica. 
Monthly mean CO concentration has generally been observed highest in the months 
of August (72.62 ± 24 ppbv), September (73.17 ± 28 ppbv) and October (73.25 ± 27 
ppbv) and minimum in the months of January (42.77 ± 15.06 ppbv) and February 
43.24 ± 14.64 ppbv). Diurnal changes were systematically observed, with higher 
CO concentration during daytime sunlit period. This CO enhancement in daytime 
sunlit period could be due to the photochemical production by photolysis of organic 
matter.
Keywords: - Carbon monoxide, snow firn, formaldehyde, solar insolation cycle.
INTRODUCTION
Photochemical reactions in snow have recently witnessed an 
unprecedented surge of interest [Couch et al., 2000, and Domine’  and 
Shepson, 2002 and many more]. Several experiments on freshly fallen snow 
[Haan et al., 2001] as well as on the artificial snow [Hutterli et al., 2002] 
are carried out in the laboratory under controlled condition. On the other 
hand numerous field studies at different locations in polar region, Arctic 
[Ridley et al., 2000, and Sumner and Shepson, 1999] as well as Antarctic, 
[Davis et al., 2001, Jones et al., 2000, and Jones et al., 2001] and mid­

latitude regions [Honrath et al., 1999, Honrath et al., 2000a, Honrath et al., 
2000b, Hutterli et al., 1999, Hutterli et al., 2001, and Jacobi et al., 2002] 
have been performed. The result obtained by Haan et al. [2001] from the 
field experiment and laboratory tests suggested that the organic compounds 
and formaldehyde photolysis could be a major substrate for the photochemical 
CO production in freshly fallen snow. At the same time Haan et al [2001] 
also observed diurnal changes in CO concentration in freshly fallen snow 
samples. Rammussen et al. [1982] observed large amounts of CO in snow 
samples collected at Mount Hood (Oregon) and attributed the abundant 
CO to the absorption of atmospheric CO molecules on snow crystals.
Riedel et al. [1999] investigated the annual cycle of formaldehyde at 
Antarctica and found that the diurnal and seasonal cycle of HCHO exists, 
with maximum in summer and minimum in winter. Further, they investigated 
that the observed concentration shows diurnal variation on clear sunny days, 
with maximum in early afternoon and minimum during night. Experimental 
results have demonstrated production of reactive nitrogen oxides in the 
surface layer of irradiated snow covers [Beine et al., 2002, Davis et al., 
2001, Honrath et al., 1999, Honrath et al., 2000a, Jones et al., 2000 and 
Jones et al., 2001 ] through photolysis of nitrate incorporated in snow [Cotter 
et al., 2003 and Honrath et al., 2000b] and are subsequently released into 
the atmosphere. Exchange of hydrogen peroxide (H2 0 2 ) and formaldehyde 
(HCHO) between the snow and the atmosphere had been reported [Hutterli 
et al., 1999, Hutterli et al., 2002, Jacobi et al., 2002 and Jacobi et al., 2003], 
Such an exchange of photo-chemically and chemically active gases modifies 
the chemical composition and the oxidation capacity of the boundary layer 
over the snow-covered regions [Ridley et al., 2000 and Yang et al., 2002],
In order to study the diurnal and seasonal pattern of CO, online 
measurements of CO were carried out at Maitri, Antarctica. Here we report 
the results obtained from 12 months of regular observation during 2004 
period, which shows the existence of diurnal and seasonal pattern of CO in 
Antarctica.
Observation site and general meteorology
The observation site Maitri, Indian Antarctic Research Station 
(hereafter, only Maitri will be mentioned) is located on a rocky, ice-free 
area called Schirmacher Oasis of Queen Mand Land, Antarctica. CO 
analyzer was installed in small hut (Environmental laboratory) located 160 
m northeast of the main station, where as the stations generator complex is 
located 50 m southwest of the main station. The second nearest local source 
of CO, Russian station’s generator complex, is located at 3.5 km southeast- 
east of main station.
